\chapter{The Multi-Criteria Benchmark}
\label{chap:benchmark}

This chapter presents the results of the benchmark of 14 tabular
models on the 18 OpenML datasets, executed under the single protocol
of Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia} --- it is the chapter that answers
RQ1 (\emph{does the accuracy tie among the families survive a
rigorous protocol and the arrival of the 2026 generation of
foundation models?}). The reading has two movements: in the core of
11 models predating the 2026 extension, the top of the accuracy
ranking is a statistical tie gauged by practical equivalence and the
model$\times$dataset interaction (together with noise) dominates the
rank variance, so that the decision migrates to cost, latency,
robustness, and task structure; the 2026 generation shifts the top
--- TabFM, zero-shot, leads the average rank in all three tasks (in
multiclass, over the two datasets where it operates), at the cost of
four to five orders of magnitude in inference latency --- a lead that
is consistent across datasets, which the underpowered tests do not
confirm as a statistical separation. The chapter also discusses the
unfavorable independent test of the Kolmogorov--Arnold family, the
conditional reversals that feed the decision framework of
Chapter~\ref{chap:framework} and, closing the chapter, the
instance-level complementarity analysis that explains \emph{where}
the shift happens.

\section{Coverage and organization of the evidence}
\label{sec:cap5-cobertura}

The benchmark completes \textbf{250 of the 252 possible cells} (14
models $\times$ 18 datasets). The two absences are documented
structural exclusions, not execution failures: the \texttt{helena}
dataset, with 100 classes, exceeds the architectural class limit of
both foundation models (TabPFN and TabFM), which therefore produce no
prediction on it. This distinction matters for the statistical
reading: cells absent due to an architectural limit are information
about the model --- a decision criterion in itself, revisited in
Chapter~\ref{chap:framework} --- and not missing data to impute. The
dataset identities are those of Table~\ref{tab:datasets}; the fifth
regression dataset of the core is \texttt{kin8nm}.

Before the results, it is worth revisiting the sample space on which
they rest. Figure~\ref{fig:dataset-landscape}, in
Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}, positions the 18 datasets on the
samples $\times$ attributes plane; here we only recall the reading
this chapter needs. It shows that the sample of datasets is not
concentrated in a single regime: there are small and large, narrow
and wide datasets, across the three tasks --- a necessary condition
for the conditional analyses of Act~III (imbalance, categorical
cardinality, size) to have variation to explore. The symmetric caveat
is also visible: with 10 binary, 3 multiclass, and 5 regression
datasets, the statistical power per task is limited, and the text
declares that limitation at every point where it binds.

Throughout the chapter, two comparison grids coexist and must be
distinguished from the start. The study's \emph{11-model core}
gathers the models predating the benchmark's 2026 extension: the
three GBDTs (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), seven deep-learning models
(MLP, FT-Transformer, SAINT, TabNet, STab, RealMLP, TabM), and one
foundation model (TabPFN). The \emph{full 14-model grid} adds the
three models incorporated in the extension: the TabFM foundation
model \citep{tabfm2026,kong2026} and the two Kolmogorov--Arnold
networks (KAN \citep{kan2024} and TabKAN \citep{tabkan2025}). The cut
is defined by the models' order of entry into the study, not by
publication year: TabPFN, a foundation model, belongs to the core.
Acts~I to III read the 11-model core --- it is on it that the maxim
``boosting always wins'' \citep{grinsztajn2022} was formulated, a
maxim \citet{mcelfresh2023} already nuanced by concluding that the
choice of dataset matters more than the choice of model --- and it is
on it that the tie is established; Act~IV reads the full grid and
shows what the extension changes; and Act~V descends to the instance
level to locate where the foundation models and the GBDTs diverge.

For this chapter's self-contained reading, it is worth recapping the
essentials of Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}: hyperparameter
selection by internal cross-validation ($3$ folds on the pool,
executed once), re-evaluation on $5$ external folds with the
configuration fixed, Bayesian tuning via Optuna/TPE \citep{akiba2019}
with a budget fixed per family (100 trials for GBDTs, 25 for DL; cost
asymmetry measured and declared in
Section~\ref{sec:met-protocolo}), a fixed 20\% hold-out (seed 42)
that no selection stage ever observes, and per-family preprocessing
(one-hot for attention, ordinal for trees, embeddings where the model
defines them). Two design asymmetries are declared because they
affect the reading of the results: the 100/25-trial budgets
\emph{attenuate} the wall-clock disparity of tuning (the design
premise estimated a DL trial at ${\sim}4\times$ a GBDT trial; the
measurements showed a larger disparity, declared in
Section~\ref{sec:met-protocolo} --- the residual bias favors DL,
which still does not win), and the foundation models enter zero-shot
--- with no tuning at all --- because that entry is the very paradigm
claim under test; their inference configurations are fixed a priori,
never tuned to our data: the 50{,}000-row context cap is TabPFN's
native limit, mirrored by us in TabFM (whose library default is
uncapped), and the 8-member ensemble is likewise our fixed choice
(TabFM's default is 32), as Section~\ref{sec:met-protocolo} declares.

\section{Act I --- the statistical tie of the 11-model core}
\label{sec:cap5-ato1}

Restricted to the 11-model core, binary classification ($N{=}10$
datasets) exhibits a statistically indistinguishable top. The omnibus
test rejects global rank equality (Friedman $\chi^2 = 31.3$,
$p = 5.2\times10^{-4}$; Iman--Davenport correction $F = 4.1$,
$p = 1.1\times10^{-4}$) --- there are, therefore, real differences
somewhere in the grid --- but the Nemenyi post-hoc \citep{demsar2006}
does not separate the leading pack: the top models fall within one
critical difference of each other. Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-cd} presents
the critical difference diagram, the canonical visual instrument of
this analysis, in which the axis is the average rank (lower is
better) and each horizontal bar connects a group of models less than
one CD apart --- hence statistically inseparable; the width of those
bars is the visual form of the caution about the wide CD that
Section~\ref{sec:cap5-ato4} revisits on the full grid.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{images/cd_diagram_binary_11.pdf}
\caption[Critical difference diagram (11-model core)]{Critical
difference diagram (Nemenyi) for binary classification in the
11-model core ($N{=}10$ datasets, $\mathrm{CD}=4.77$). What to look
at: TabPFN leads the average rank (3.2), but the top bar connects
TabPFN all the way to the MLP --- the post-hoc does not separate the
pack, which is why the equivalence reading comes from the Bayesian
instrument, not from here.}
\label{fig:cap5-cd}
\end{figure}

The interpretation demands an immediate caveat: a post-hoc that does
not separate is not, by itself, evidence of equivalence --- with
large $k$ and small $N$, the critical difference is wide by
construction, and ``not separable'' may mean only ``no power to
separate''. That is exactly why the protocol adds finer instruments,
presented in Chapter~\ref{chap:fundamentacao} and applied next; they
were defined after the analysis of the results had begun and are not
part of a pre-registration.

The Bayesian signed-rank test with a region of practical equivalence
(ROPE) \citep{benavoli2017} answers the question the frequentist one
cannot reach: what is the probability that the difference between two
models is \emph{practically irrelevant}? The criterion and the
quantity must come declared, because two conventions coexist: this
analysis uses the \emph{expected posterior mass} in each region
($E[\theta]$) with a 0.5 cutoff; the convention of
\citet{benavoli2017} uses the fraction of posterior samples in which
the region is the most probable, typically with a 0.95 cutoff. With a
ROPE of $\pm$0.01 AUC, \textbf{8 of the 10} non-leading models of the
core have $E[\theta_{\mathrm{ROPE}}] > 0.5$ against the rank leader
(TabPFN) --- one of them, the MLP, exactly at the bar (0.508). Under
the Benavoli convention the count at the 0.5 cutoff is the same, but
at the strict 0.95 cutoff only \textbf{3 of the 10} reach it ---
XGBoost (0.999), LightGBM (0.992), and CatBoost (0.957), the three
GBDTs --- and, in the opposite direction, no model reaches 0.95 of
practical \emph{superiority} over the leader (a single one, TabNet,
reaches 0.95 of inferiority). In plain language: the strict criterion
licenses saying that the three GBDTs and TabPFN are practically
equivalent in AUC within one percentage point; the lenient criterion
($E[\theta]>0.5$) says only that, for the others, equivalence is more
probable than the two alternatives combined --- a much weaker claim,
and it is with it that the count reaches 8 of 10. The threshold
sensitivity analysis shows the progression
$0.005/0.01/0.02 \to 2/8/10$ equivalents under the $E[\theta]>0.5$
criterion (and $0/3/5$ under the strict one): the tie conclusion
holds within one percentage point of AUC, stronger for the GBDTs than
for the networks. On the $E[\theta]$ reading, XGBoost ($0.65$) clears
the 0.5 bar even at the strict 0.005 threshold, with CatBoost at the
edge (0.54). The tie at the top is therefore not an artifact of low
power: it is practical equivalence positively gauged --- under the
criteria declared above
(\texttt{results/\allowbreak aggregated/\allowbreak rope\_\allowbreak sensitivity.csv}).
The paired effect sizes (Cohen's $d$ on the per-dataset AUC
differences; item 5 of the protocol of
Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}) tell the same story on another
yardstick: within the pack, effects are small to medium (TabPFN $-$
XGBoost $d{=}0.28$), grow at the generation frontier (TabFM $-$
XGBoost $d{=}0.68$), and only become large against the tail of the
grid (TabNet $-$ TabPFN $d{=}{-}1.54$); the complete matrices, binary
and regression, and the bootstrap intervals of the mean AUC (item 6
of the protocol) are in Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas}, next to the
secondary-metric rank tables and the across-fold variability.

\emph{In the 11-model core, the top of binary classification is a
statistical tie: 8 of the 10 non-leading models are practically
equivalent to the leader under a ROPE of $\pm$0.01 AUC on the
$E[\theta]>0.5$ criterion --- 3 of the 10, the GBDTs, at the strict
0.95 cutoff --- and the conclusion survives variation of the
threshold.} The omnibus rejects global equality, but the post-hoc
does not separate the leading pack and the Bayesian instrument
declares practical equivalence --- the maxim ``boosting always wins''
finds, in this generation, no accuracy margin to support it.

An honest delimitation before proceeding: the tie is established in
binary classification, the only task with enough $N$ ($N{=}10$) for
the instruments to operate with useful power. In regression, $N{=}5$
imposes a combinatorial floor on the paired Wilcoxon p-value (0.0625
--- no comparison can cross the conventional 5\% threshold there, by
arithmetic, not by absence of effect); in multiclass, $N{=}3$ reduces
any analysis to the descriptive plane. These limitations are declared
in every section where they become binding, and no central conclusion
of this chapter depends on significance in a task without power to
gauge it.

If the top ties, the remaining question is what, after all, explains
the rank variation that does exist. Since ranks are assigned within
each dataset, all the variance splits between what is attributable to
the model and a residual. The model's identity accounts for 0.31 of
the total: 0.20 is difference between families and 0.11 difference
between models of the same family (of the model share, the family
accounts for 64.5\%). The residual, 0.69, is the part in which the
same model changes position from one dataset to another; with a
single value per model$\times$dataset, it bundles the
model$\times$dataset interaction and the measurement noise, which we
cannot separate. The reading the numbers support is therefore: a
model's average position predicts less than a third of the rank
variation, and most of it depends on the dataset --- the ``GBDT vs.\
DL'' axis is a weak abstraction not because the family matters little
relative to the model, but because both are small relative to the
residual. One caveat: with the core's unbalanced families (3 GBDTs, 7
DL, 1 foundation model), the share attributable to the family is
mechanically limited.

\emph{The model's identity accounts for 0.31 of the rank variance
(0.20 from the family, 0.11 from the model-within-family); the
remaining 0.69 --- interaction with the dataset plus noise --- varies
from dataset to dataset: the winner depends on the dataset.} This
finding reorients the practical question from ``which family?'' to
``which model, under which constraints?'' --- the seed of the
framework of Chapter~\ref{chap:framework}.

The critical difference diagram and the $\eta^2$ operate on
aggregated ranks; neither shows the absolute magnitudes nor where,
dataset by dataset, the differences live.
Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-heatmap} fills that gap with the classification
heat map: the primary metric per model (columns) and dataset (rows)
--- ROC-AUC on the binary datasets (higher is better) and log-loss on
the multiclass ones (lower is better) --- so that the two metrics
coexist on the same grid and the valid comparison is within each row,
never across rows.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/heatmap_classification_en.pdf}
\caption[Classification heat map]{Primary metric per model (columns,
grouped by family and ordered by average rank) and dataset (rows):
ROC-AUC on binary, log-loss on multiclass. Color encodes the model's
\emph{rank within the dataset} (1 = best, darkest), so the valid
comparison --- within each row --- is the one the color shows; the
absolute values are annotated. The dashes in \texttt{helena} are the
two structural exclusions.}
\label{fig:cap5-heatmap}
\end{figure}

The per-dataset reading confirms the aggregate one --- small margins
at the top of the binary datasets --- and adds what the aggregate
does not show: the two structurally empty cells become visible, and
the few datasets where one model opens a clear advantage (such as
CatBoost on \texttt{amazon\_\allowbreak employee}, of high
categorical cardinality) anticipate the conditional reversals of
Act~III. The caveat stands: hold-out values on a single fixed
partition carry no significance by themselves --- they illustrate;
the inference pairs the datasets (one hold-out value per dataset, as
Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia} fixes), and the folds feed only the
variability table of Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas}.

While the top ties, the bottom does not: TabNet \citep{arik2021} is
consistently the worst model of the core generation, with average
ranks of 11.8 (binary), 11.7 (multiclass), and 11.4 (regression) on
the full grid. It is the only raw-performance verdict the benchmark
licenses without qualification within the core --- and a reminder
that architectures celebrated in the literature may not survive a
uniform protocol with per-family tuning budgets and paired
conditions.

\section{Act II --- the cost axes}
\label{sec:cap5-ato2}

If accuracy ties, the decision among the top models needs other axes
--- and it is on them that the models differ radically. This section
walks the three cost axes measured by the protocol (training time,
hyperparameter tuning cost, and inference latency) and crosses them
with performance on the Pareto frontier.

Median training time varies about $300\times$ among the actually
trained models of the grid: LightGBM and XGBoost fit the final model
in ${\sim}0.7$~s, while SAINT and STab consume ${\sim}200$~s per fit
--- and the difference multiplies by the number of tuning trials and
cross-validation folds. The foundation models invert the axis: being
zero-shot, TabFM's ``training'' costs 0.18~s and TabPFN's 1.35~s,
with \textbf{zero} tuning cost --- there is no hyperparameter search
to pay for. This inversion, whose other side appears in the very next
paragraph, is the thread that stitches the chapter together.

The second axis is the total cost of hyperparameter tuning, which the
training time of a single fit underestimates. In the across-dataset
medians (excluding \texttt{adult}, per the cost protocol of
Section~\ref{sec:met-protocolo}), the GBDTs pay from 104~s (LightGBM)
to 646~s (CatBoost) for the full search cycle; MLP-style DL pays from
1{,}117~s (MLP) to 2{,}242~s (TabM); and heavy attention reaches
9{,}831~s (SAINT) and 14{,}622~s (STab) --- two orders of magnitude
above the cheapest GBDTs to, as seen in Act~I, not leave the tie (the
consolidated cost table is in Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas}). The
foundation models pay zero. This axis rarely appears in the
literature's benchmarks, but it is what the practitioner pays at
every model refresh in production.

Inference latency is the benchmark's most dramatic axis.
Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-latencia} presents the complete measurement,
done under an identical protocol for the 14 models: \us{} per row (on
a logarithmic scale in the figure; lower is better), median of 5
passes over the full \texttt{adult} hold-out, each model on its
natural device (GBDTs on CPU; deep models and foundation models on
GPU).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{images/inference_time.pdf}
\caption[Inference latency on \texttt{adult}]{Inference latency on
\texttt{adult}, in \us{} per row (median of 5 passes, log scale;
colors by family). Source:
\texttt{results/\allowbreak latency/\allowbreak latency\_\allowbreak adult.\allowbreak csv}.}
\label{fig:cap5-latencia}
\end{figure}

The figure's structure organizes into four layers. At the base,
XGBoost serves at 0.33~\us/row. The fast tier gathers the three
GBDTs, the MLP-style deep models, and the two KANs (CatBoost 1.4;
RealMLP 1.5; LightGBM 1.9; TabKAN 2.3; MLP 2.4; KAN 3.1; TabM
3.5~\us/row) --- a result in itself: deep learning is \emph{not}
synonymous with expensive serving; the architecture decides.
Attention costs tens of microseconds (TabNet 17; FT-Transformer 29;
SAINT 45). And the extreme belongs to the structurally
inference-heavy paradigms: TabPFN 7{,}416, STab 8{,}645, and TabFM
43{,}262~\us/row --- STab's cost comes from the Bayesian inference
that averages 64 stochastic passes; the foundation models', from
carrying the training set as context on every prediction. The regime
caveat deserves emphasis: these ratios describe amortized batch
serving on the hardware declared in Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia};
single-row online serving narrows the differences --- but not the
orders of magnitude. The measured factors are TabPFN $22{,}473\times$
and TabFM $131{,}097\times$ XGBoost on \texttt{adult} --- and the
ratio varies with the dataset, from $3{,}079\times$
(\texttt{credit\_g}) to $247{,}402\times$
(\texttt{cardiovascular\_\allowbreak disease}) in the multi-dataset
measurement
(\texttt{results/\allowbreak latency/\allowbreak latency\_\allowbreak multi.csv}),
which is why no single factor should be quoted without its dataset.

None of the isolated axes decides; the decision instrument is the
performance $\times$ cost cross. On average rank $\times$ cost ---
rank being the study's primary comparison instrument --- the 11-model
core resolves into a Pareto frontier of \{TabPFN, XGBoost, LightGBM\}
on the training-cost axis (medians over the 18 datasets,
Table~\ref{tab:app-custos}: LightGBM 0.66~s, XGBoost 0.69~s, TabPFN
1.35~s), which narrows to \{XGBoost, TabPFN\} on the latency axis (on
mean AUC instead of rank, CatBoost also joins the frontier --- and,
on the latency axis, TabPFN leaves it); \textbf{all classical deep
learning is dominated} in both crosses.
Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-pareto} presents the complete picture, already
with the 14 models, on both planes; on the full grid of the training
panel, the frontier reduces to TabFM itself, which combines the best
rank with the lowest median training time.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/pareto_binary_en.pdf}
\caption[Pareto frontiers: rank $\times$ cost]{Pareto frontiers on
the mean binary rank $\times$ cost plane: (a) median training time
over the 18 datasets --- 17 for the foundation models --- (the same
base as Table~\ref{tab:app-custos}); (b) inference latency on
\texttt{adult}. The rank axis is inverted (up-left is better); stars
mark the frontier of the full 14-model grid, and the dashed line
joins the frontier of the 11-model core, whose membership is decided
on the ranks recomputed within the cut. What to look at: in panel (a)
TabFM dominates the grid alone and the core resolves into \{LightGBM,
XGBoost, TabPFN\}; in panel (b) the picture inverts --- the frontier
becomes \{XGBoost, TabPFN, TabFM\}, with the foundation models paying
four to five orders of magnitude of latency for the rank.}
\label{fig:cap5-pareto}
\end{figure}

The figure shows what latency alone does not: on the training
$\times$ rank plane, the foundation models occupy the optimal corner
--- and it is only when the cost axis switches to serving latency
that the picture inverts. This double reading is the
\textbf{chapter's central finding}: the in-context-learning paradigm
buys seconds-long training and zero tuning at the price of an
inference latency four to five orders of magnitude higher on
\texttt{adult}. It is what motivates both the constraint axis of the
decision framework (Chapter~\ref{chap:framework}) and the
distillation question (Chapter~\ref{chap:destilacao}): how much of
that price is removable?

\emph{Models practically equivalent in accuracy (under the lenient
criterion) differ by up to ${\sim}300\times$ in training time and by
more than four orders of magnitude in inference latency; in the
11-model core, the rank~$\times$~cost Pareto frontier is \{TabPFN,
XGBoost, LightGBM\} on the training axis --- and all classical deep
learning is dominated.} When performance ties, cost decides --- and
cost does not tie.

\section{Act III --- conditional reversals and the size axis}
\label{sec:cap5-ato3}

The tie of Act~I is an aggregate picture; it does not imply that all
problems are alike. This act conditions the results on task structure
and sample size, and finds real reversals --- the raw material of the
constraint questions of Chapter~\ref{chap:framework}.

In multiclass classification, the deep models of the most recent
generation (STab and TabM, both with average rank 3.67 on the full
grid) take the classical top from the GBDTs (XGBoost, the best of
them, sits at 6.0). The power caveat is binding and repeated whenever
multiclass appears: with $N{=}3$ datasets, the analysis is
\textbf{descriptive} --- there is no test with useful power on three
points --- and therefore no central conclusion rests exclusively on
it.

The second reversal appears when the classification datasets are
stratified by imbalance ratio. Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-imbalance}
presents the average ranks aggregated by family (lower is better;
axis inverted in the figure) in three severity bands of the
majority/minority ratio: mild ($<$2:1), moderate (2--5:1), and severe
($\geq$5:1).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{images/imbalance_robustness.png}
\caption[Robustness to imbalance]{Robustness to imbalance: average
rank aggregated by family and severity band on the classification
datasets. Source:
\texttt{results/\allowbreak figures/\allowbreak imbalance\_\allowbreak robustness.\allowbreak png}
(\texttt{notebooks/\allowbreak 07\_\allowbreak segmented\_\allowbreak robustness.\allowbreak ipynb}).}
\label{fig:cap5-imbalance}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-imbalance} shows two opposite trends, on the
ranks of the full 14-model grid: the GBDTs' average rank improves as
imbalance grows (6.6 in the mild band; 5.5 in the moderate; 4.6 in
the severe), the deep models' worsens (8.7 $\to$ 8.9 $\to$ 9.6), and
the foundation models stay ahead in all three bands, with no defined
trend (3.3; 4.1; 2.7). With 3, 4, and 3 datasets per band, this is a
descriptive direction, not a test. Two observations complete the
conditional picture. At the categorical-cardinality extreme
(\texttt{amazon\_\allowbreak employee}), the attention models sit at
the bottom of the table (Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-heatmap}); the one-hot
encoding and the 50-category-per-column cap
(Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}) are candidate explanations, not
tested causes. And TabPFN combines, within the core and considering
the three tasks jointly, the best average rank with the best worst
rank over the 17 datasets where it operates --- on none of them does
it fall to the bottom of the table, an attribute the average rank
alone does not capture (in classification alone, XGBoost's worst case
is equal or better).

None of the previous analyses answers the practitioner's most
frequent question: ``with \emph{my} data volume, who wins?''. The
learning curves --- 6 models $\times$ 5 datasets $\times$ 3 seeds,
sweeping from 500 samples to the full pool --- give that axis shape.
Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-curvas} presents the full sweep: each panel
names its metric and direction, the bands are $\pm$1 standard
deviation over the seeds, and a crossover is the point where one
family's curve permanently crosses the other's.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/learning_curves_diss.pdf}
\caption[Learning curves --- 6 models, 5 datasets]{Learning curves of
6 models on 5 datasets, from 500 samples to the full pool (3 seeds).
Source:
\texttt{scripts/\allowbreak fig\_\allowbreak learning\_\allowbreak curves\_\allowbreak diss.\allowbreak py}
on \texttt{results/\allowbreak learning\_\allowbreak curve/\allowbreak curve.\allowbreak csv}.}
\label{fig:cap5-curvas}
\end{figure}

Three readings come out of the figure. First: the leadership
crossover between GBDTs and DL exists, but is dataset-specific --- on
3 of the 5 swept datasets (\texttt{higgs}, \texttt{jannis}, and
\texttt{year\_\allowbreak prediction}), DL overtakes the GBDTs and
does not give the lead back; on \texttt{adult}, the GBDT retakes it
at $n \approx 4{,}000$; and on
\texttt{give\_\allowbreak me\_\allowbreak some\_\allowbreak credit},
the GBDT leads from start to finish. There is, therefore, no
universal ``critical $n$'' to recommend: the honest answer to the
practitioner is that the crossover depends on the dataset, not only
on the size. Second: TabPFN has the best average regime metric on the
five swept datasets for $n \leq 4{,}000$ (average rank 1.0 in that
regime, against XGBoost's 2.8) --- the quantification of the
zero-shot paradigm's strength in the low-data regime (a result of
subsampling \emph{within} each dataset; it does not confine the
foundation models' advantage to small datasets --- see
Section~\ref{sec:cap5-ato5}). Third, the caveat: the sweep covers 6
of the 14 models and 5 of the 18 datasets; it qualifies the size
axis, it does not reorder it.

\emph{The best family depends on the problem's structure --- recent
DL takes the multiclass top (descriptive), the GBDTs gain relative
advantage under severe imbalance, attention sinks at the categorical
extreme --- and the GBDT$\leftrightarrow$DL size crossover is real
but dataset-specific, with TabPFN dominating the $n \leq 4{,}000$
regime on all swept datasets.} The reversals do not restore the maxim
of a single winning family: they show that the right answer is
conditional --- and conditions verifiable a priori are exactly what a
decision framework can encode.

\section{Act IV --- the shift of the top: the 2026 generation}
\label{sec:cap5-ato4}

The expansion to the full 14-model grid changes the picture. TabFM
--- a foundation model released in June 2026, evaluated here
zero-shot, with no per-dataset tuning --- leads the average rank
\textbf{in all three tasks}: 2.7 in binary, 1.0 in multiclass (a
perfect score over its two eligible datasets; \texttt{helena} is a
structural exclusion), and 1.2 in regression. It is the absolute best
model on \textbf{13 of the 18 datasets}, competing in 17.
Table~\ref{tab:cap5-ranks} summarizes the ranks per task; the
complete master table, with each model's primary metric on each of
the 18 datasets, is in Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas}.
Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-ranks} presents the visual picture, in which the
binary and regression panels cover the 14 models and the multiclass
panel shows the 12 models evaluated on the three multiclass datasets,
ranked within that subset --- and therefore not directly comparable
to the table's 14-model ranks, in which the foundation models
(excluded on \texttt{helena}) are ranked.

Two concrete details give the lead scale. In multiclass, where the
margin is most visible, TabFM reaches a log-loss of 0.0966 on
\texttt{covertype} and 0.5709 on \texttt{jannis}, against 0.1644 for
the runner-up on \texttt{covertype} (TabPFN) and 0.6583 for TabPFN on
\texttt{jannis} (third there; second is TabM, at 0.6572) --- margins
visibly larger than those separating rank neighbors within the
11-model core in the same table (Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas}). One
boundary condition is declared on \texttt{covertype}: the dataset has
581 thousand rows and the protocol subsamples it to 100{,}000 (a cap
fixed before the foundation models entered and identical for the 14
models); TabFM's win holds in that regime, and we did not measure
what the tuned models would reach with the full base --- the cap is
justified in Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia} by feasibility and
parity. And TabPFN, in turn, consolidates as the grid's consistent
runner-up (average ranks 4.2/2.5/3.0 in the three tasks): the result
is not confined to one model --- the two foundation models occupy the
top two posts in every task.

Regression, the task with the fewest datasets, deserves its own
paragraph. On the full grid, the order of the average RMSE ranks is
TabFM (1.2), TabPFN (3.0), XGBoost (5.0), RealMLP (5.2), LightGBM
(5.6), and CatBoost (5.8) (Table~\ref{tab:app-regressao}); MAE and
R\textsuperscript{2} preserve the top two places
(Table~\ref{tab:app-secundarias-regression}). With five datasets, no
paired test can reach 5\% significance, and the reading is
descriptive. In binary classification, the KS statistic, usual in
credit, gives the same order at the top as ROC-AUC: TabFM (3.0),
TabPFN (4.8), and XGBoost (5.0) (Table~\ref{tab:app-ks}).

The interpretive consequence is the re-scoping of Act~I: the tie is
correctly read as a \emph{picture of the previous generation}. What
overtook the GBDTs was not a model trained on the task, but a
pre-trained model used without tuning --- the association with
pre-training is a description of what is measured, not a tested
mechanism. And the statistical caution remains stated: with $k{=}14$
and $N{=}10$, the Nemenyi critical difference is wide
(Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-cd14}) --- TabFM's separation rests on the
consistency across datasets (13 wins out of 18) and on the paired
effect sizes ($d=0.68$ against XGBoost), \textbf{not} on the
frequentist post-hoc \emph{nor} on the Bayesian instrument: against
XGBoost, the Benavoli convention puts 0.67 of the posterior
probability on TabFM's superiority (0.33 on equivalence; expected
posterior mass of equivalence $E[\theta]=0.40$), and against CatBoost
the modal region is equivalence --- consistency, without decisive
statistical separation. Three additional boundary conditions are
declared: in regression, $N{=}5$ puts the Wilcoxon p-value floor at
0.0625 (a combinatorial floor --- no result can be ``significant at
5\%'' there); one of the five regression datasets is the
binarized-target \texttt{california\_\allowbreak housing} of the
erratum (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) --- the sensitivity is innocuous
here: without it, the leaders do not change (TabFM 1.25, TabPFN
3.25) and only XGBoost (5.0${\to}$5.5) and RealMLP (4.75) swap
positions mid-grid; and TabFM is evaluated at the pinned v1.0.1
version (July 2026), whose official technical report appeared only in
late September 2026 \citep{kong2026} and remains without peer review
--- the results are about that version, and this is recorded.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{images/cd_diagram_binary.pdf}
\caption[Critical difference diagram (14-model grid)]{Critical
difference diagram (Nemenyi) for binary classification on the full
14-model grid ($N{=}10$ datasets, $\mathrm{CD}=6.27$). With $k{=}14$,
the critical difference spans nearly half the axis: the instrument
has no power to separate TabFM from the pack, and the reading of the
lead rests on consistency across datasets and on effect sizes.}
\label{fig:cap5-cd14}
\end{figure}

The counterweight is frontal, and it is the chapter's central
finding: the accuracy leader is the grid's worst model in serving
latency --- 43{,}262~\us/row under the standard protocol,
$131{,}097\times$ XGBoost, and more in larger contexts, reaching
${\sim}394$~ms/row on the largest regression dataset. The decision
question has changed its nature: it is no longer ``which family
wins?'' but ``\emph{does the foundation model's latency fit the use
case?}''.

\emph{The 2026 generation shifts the top: TabFM leads the average
rank in all three tasks (in multiclass, over 2 datasets) and is the
best model on 13 of the 18 datasets, zero-shot --- a consistent lead,
which the underpowered tests do not confirm as a statistical
separation --- at the price of four to five orders of magnitude in
serving latency (43{,}262 vs.\ 0.33~\us/row).} The tie did not make
the multi-criteria framework obsolete; the shift made it more
necessary --- and pointed to its single obstacle.

In the same movement of the extension, the benchmark produces the
independent test of the Kolmogorov--Arnold family --- and the result
is the negative of value. KAN (ranks 11.0/12.0/9.8 in
binary/multiclass/regression) and TabKAN (11.4/13.3/11.8) occupy the
bottom third in all three tasks, with TabKAN behind even TabNet in
multiclass and regression. Surprising in light of the original
papers' claims \citep{kan2024,tabkan2025}, the result calls for
explanation. Under a uniform protocol with per-family tuning budgets,
the claims do not reproduce --- with the caveat, declared in
Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}, that TabKAN is our own
reimplementation (AdamW with mini-batches in place of the original
L-BFGS) and KAN had its normalization and grid range adapted: a weak
performance by a reimplemented model confounds the quality of the
method with that of the implementation, and the conclusion holds for
this grid's protocol. A compatible explanation, not tested here, is
that the original comparisons used undertuned baselines --- a reading
consistent with the cost-parity critique \citep{kancritical2024} and
with the fact that \citet{poeta2024}, without GBDT baselines and with
ten-epoch training, reached results \emph{favorable} to KAN in
accuracy: an undertuned comparison favors whoever trains faster. As
far as our dated novelty check reaches, this is the family's first
test against the full GBDT/DL/foundation-model grid in a
multi-criteria tabular benchmark; the previous independent
evaluations \citep{poeta2024,kancritical2024} compare KANs only
against MLPs and do not measure cost axes. The engineering
counterpart deserves symmetric record: both inhabit the fast latency
tier (2.3--3.1~\us/row) --- \textbf{the problem is the performance,
not the cost}.

\emph{Under a uniform protocol, KAN and TabKAN sit in the bottom
third in all three tasks --- the original papers' claims do not hold
up in the first independent test against the full grid, as far as our
dated check reaches --- though both are cheap to serve.} The negative
result is reported with the same status as the positive ones, per the
study's conduct contract (Chapter~\ref{chap:metodologia}): a neutral
benchmark exists precisely so that results like this become public.

\section{Act V --- inside the scoreboard: instance-level complementarity}
\label{sec:cap5-ato5}

Average ranks say \emph{who} wins; they do not say \emph{where} or
\emph{why}. To separate the two questions --- what XGBoost already
learns on its own and what the foundation models add --- this section
descends to the instance level: the case-by-case predictions of
XGBoost, TabPFN, and TabFM on the untouched hold-out, on the 17
datasets where the three coexist. The design was pre-registered
\emph{before} execution, with dated hypotheses and falsification
criteria
(\texttt{docs/\allowbreak desenho-\allowbreak analise-\allowbreak complementaridade.\allowbreak md},
2026-10-22; execution addendum of 2026-10-23), and the generation of
the predictions rebuilt the final models under the benchmark's exact
protocol --- same chosen hyperparameters, same split, same seed ---
with a sanity gate requiring $|\Delta| \le 10^{-3}$ between the
recomputed primary metric and the recorded one: all 52 cells passed,
42 of them with exact $\Delta = 0$; the rest fall between $10^{-7}$
and $6 \times 10^{-6}$ (TabPFN numerical noise), with a single case
at $4.8 \times 10^{-4}$ (\emph{bfloat16} under a reduced prediction
batch in TabFM). The per-pair instrument is McNemar's exact test
\citep{mcnemar1947} on the discordant instances, accompanied by the
agreement rate and the win balance per quintile of XGBoost's margin
--- a binary instance's \emph{margin} is $|\hat p - 0.5|$, the
distance of the predicted probability from the point of indecision:
low margin means the tree hesitates.

The four hypotheses, all directional and with dated falsification
criteria, deserve explicit statement, because the verdicts below are
measured against them. \textbf{H-C1} (dominant redundancy): the
models share most of the signal --- label agreement above 85\% in
the median across datasets; refuted if below. \textbf{H-C2} (the
gain lives in uncertainty): the FM's wins concentrate where XGBoost
hesitates --- a larger balance in the lowest-margin quintile than in
the highest, in most binary datasets (one-sided sign test,
$\alpha=0.05$). \textbf{H-C3} (minority class): the FM's balance is
larger on the rare class than on the majority one, in most binary
datasets (same test). \textbf{H-C4} (echo of the learning curves):
the FM's advantage \emph{decreases} with the training pool size ---
as the pre-training prior with limited context would suggest ---
i.e., negative Spearman between size and advantage over the 17
cells. The interpretation was committed upfront in the
pre-registration: confirming H-C1 with H-C2/H-C3 would support ``the
FM adds information in the uncertainty and minority regions'';
refuting them would displace the explanation elsewhere.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/complementarity_diss.pdf}
\caption[Instance-level complementarity]{Instance-level
complementarity on the hold-out: (a)~net FM wins per 1{,}000
instances (asterisk: McNemar $p<0.01$); (b)~balance per quintile of
XGBoost's margin on the 10 binary datasets. Source:
\texttt{results/\allowbreak complementarity/}.}
\label{fig:cap5-complementaridade}
\end{figure}

The first result is the scale of the agreement (hypothesis~H-C1,
\textbf{confirmed}): XGBoost and the foundation models give the same
answer in the vast majority of cases --- median agreement of 0.950
with TabPFN and 0.936 with TabFM, above the pre-registered criterion
of 0.85. The accuracy dispute therefore concentrates in a
\emph{fringe} of 0.6 to 15.5\% discordant instances per dataset.
What happens inside that fringe is asymmetric and strongly
heterogeneous across datasets
(Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-complementaridade}a): in 14 of the 24 pairs
McNemar rejects the tie at 1\%, and the median balance is $+6.6$ net
wins per 1{,}000 instances for TabFM ($+2.8$ for TabPFN). At the
extremes, TabFM converts the fringe overwhelmingly on
\texttt{jannis} ($+59.6$ per thousand, $p \sim 10^{-103}$),
\texttt{magictelescope} ($+43.3$), \texttt{phoneme} ($+37.9$),
\texttt{covertype} ($+33.7$, $p \sim 10^{-94}$), and \texttt{higgs}
($+26.0$, $p \sim 10^{-25}$) --- but \emph{loses} the fringe on
\texttt{telco\_\allowbreak customer\_\allowbreak churn} ($-29.8$,
$p = 6 \times 10^{-4}$), just as TabPFN loses it on \texttt{adult}
($-8.2$, $p = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$). The foundation models' aggregate
win is therefore not uniform dominance: it is a sum of large local
wins and real local defeats.

The three pre-registered mechanistic hypotheses \textbf{were not
confirmed} under the dated criteria --- the honest statistical
label, since none of the tests reaches significance to reject in the
opposite direction either --- and recording these negatives is as
informative as the confirmation. H-C2 (the gain concentrates at
XGBoost's low margin) fails as a universal pattern: 5/10 binary
datasets for TabPFN and 7/10 for TabFM, non-significant signs ---
though the directional picture exists
(Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-complementaridade}b): in XGBoost's most
uncertain quintile the TabFM median is $+19.5$ per thousand against
${\sim}0$ in the other quintiles, with enormous dispersion across
datasets. H-C3 (disproportionate gain on the minority class) stands
at 6/10 and 8/10 ($p = 0.055$ for TabFM --- marginal, not
conclusive); the extreme case remains eloquent --- on
\texttt{amazon\_\allowbreak employee}, 16.3:1 imbalance, TabFM's
balance on the minority class is $+266$ per 1{,}000 minority
instances, against $-10$ on the majority --- but it does not
generalize to the population. And H-C4 (the advantage decreases with
pool size, as pre-training on tables of up to 16{,}384 rows would
suggest --- though inference accepts contexts of up to 50{,}000;
Section~\ref{sec:fund-fm}) is not confirmed, with a descriptive sign
\emph{contrary} in the aggregate: the Spearman correlation between
pool size and advantage is $+0.14$ (TabPFN) and $+0.26$ (TabFM),
non-significant (restricted to the binary datasets, the AUC
advantage of \emph{TabPFN} goes in the hypothesis's direction,
$\rho=-0.61$, $p=0.060$, also non-significant --- the mixing of
metrics across tasks is part of what the aggregate dilutes) ---
descriptively, the largest balance is on \texttt{jannis} (the 5th
largest dataset of the grid), but the next posts belong to one
medium and one small dataset (\texttt{magictelescope},
\texttt{phoneme}): the reading the data support is that the
advantage \emph{does not shrink} with size, not that it grows with
it. The natural worry that the foundation model only shines in the
low-data regime finds no support here.

The same per-instance predictions allow opening the three models'
confusion matrices and translating those balances into the
operational language of Section~\ref{sec:fund-metricas-clf} ---
precision, recall, and balanced accuracy at the standard threshold,
with the minority class as the class of interest
(Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-operacionais};
Table~\ref{tab:app-operacionais} of Appendix~\ref{app:tabelas};
artifact
\texttt{secondary\_\allowbreak metrics\_\allowbreak holdout.csv}).
The translation is instructive twice over. On
\texttt{amazon\_\allowbreak employee}
(Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-operacionais}a), the accuracies are nearly
indistinguishable (0.943 to 0.949), but the minority-class recall
jumps from 0.032 (XGBoost) to 0.214 (TabPFN) and 0.298 (TabFM) ---
XGBoost detects 3 in every 100 requests that should be denied;
TabFM, 30 --- at the price of some precision (0.706 against 0.621):
in an application where the false negative is the expensive error,
the difference accuracy cannot see is the one that matters. And on
\texttt{telco\_\allowbreak customer\_\allowbreak churn} the choice of
metric \emph{inverts the verdict}: TabFM loses the fringe on McNemar
and loses in accuracy (0.771 against 0.801), but has the highest
minority recall (0.663 against 0.570) and the highest balanced
accuracy (0.737 against 0.727) --- the net-balance ``loser'' is the
model that finds the most customers at risk of churning. Panel~(b)
of Figure~\ref{fig:cap5-operacionais} places the two cases among the
10 binary datasets: on the balanced datasets the three models
practically coincide in minority recall, and the largest separations
appear on imbalanced datasets (\texttt{amazon\_\allowbreak employee},
\texttt{telco}, \texttt{bank\_\allowbreak marketing}) --- though not
on all: on
\texttt{give\_\allowbreak me\_\allowbreak some\_\allowbreak credit},
with 6.7\% minority, the three recalls differ by less than 0.02. In
balanced accuracy, incidentally, TabFM is the best of the three on 9
of the 10 binary datasets. None of these numbers ranks models ---
the threshold was not optimized and the cost of each error belongs
to the application --- but they make concrete what the chapter's
multi-criteria thesis states in the abstract: which model ``wins''
depends on the metric the application has reasons to maximize, and
an honest benchmark reports both layers instead of choosing for the
application.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/metricas_operacionais_diss.pdf}
\caption[Operational reading of the fringe]{Operational reading:
(a)~accuracy and minority recall on \texttt{amazon\_employee};
(b)~minority recall on the 10 binary datasets (internal labels in
Portuguese; EN regeneration pending in the figure pass). Source:
\texttt{results/aggregated/}.}
\label{fig:cap5-operacionais}
\end{figure}

In regression, the instance-level reading is descriptive and points
in the same double direction: the foundation model's absolute error
is smaller than XGBoost's on more than half the instances in 9 of
the 10 pairs, but the two models' errors are co-ranked (Spearman
0.33 to 0.95 per dataset; median 0.83) --- the two models find
\emph{the same} instances hard, and the FM's advantage is a nearly
uniform shrinkage of the error, not the resolution of a distinct
class of cases.

This act's interpretive synthesis corrects the easy explanation.
What the foundation model adds is \textbf{not} a universal talent
for ``the hard cases'': it is an inductive bias that suits some
datasets --- typically the dense, numeric, multiclass ones (an
\emph{a posteriori} descriptive reading, not a routing rule) ---
where it converts the disagreement fringe almost entirely in its
favor --- and unhelps on others, where XGBoost remains the fringe's
owner. For practical decision-making, the consequence is direct and
feeds Chapter~\ref{chap:framework}: with median agreement above
0.93 and an advantage whose sign changes from dataset to dataset ---
without margin or class predicting it stably --- model choice is, in
practice, a per-dataset/task decision, not a per-instance one ---
and the framework's blind evaluation is what should capture it.

\emph{At the instance level, XGBoost and the foundation models agree
on ${\ge}93.6\%$ of cases (median; H-C1 confirmed); the rank
difference arises from a disputed fringe that TabFM wins
overwhelmingly on some datasets and loses on others, and the three
pre-registered mechanistic explanations --- low margin, minority
class, little data --- were not confirmed under the dated criteria,
the last with a contrary descriptive sign in the aggregate: the
advantage does not shrink on the large datasets.}

\section{Chapter summary}
\label{sec:cap5-sintese}

RQ1 asked whether the accuracy tie among the families of tabular
models survives a rigorous protocol and the arrival of the 2026
generation of foundation models. The answer has three parts.

\textbf{Before TabFM, yes, in binary classification.} In the
11-model cut, the three GBDTs are practically equivalent to the rank
leader (TabPFN) under the strict criterion (equivalence probability
of at least 0.95 with a ROPE of $\pm0.01$ AUC), and 8 of the 10
non-leaders are under the more lenient criterion ($E[\theta]>0.5$)
--- a conclusion robust to threshold variation for the top quartet.
The model$\times$dataset interaction, together with noise, dominates
the rank variance (0.69); rational decision-making therefore
migrates to cost, latency, robustness, and task structure, exactly
the axes on which the models differ by orders of magnitude. In
multiclass ($N{=}3$) and regression ($N{=}5$), the benchmark has no
power to affirm or deny the tie.

\textbf{With TabFM, no.} It leads the average rank in all three
tasks (in multiclass, over the two datasets where it operates) and
is the best model on 13 of the 18 datasets, with no per-dataset
tuning. That lead rests on consistency across datasets and on the
effect size ($d{=}0.68$ against XGBoost); neither the frequentist
post-hoc nor the Bayesian test separates it decisively. The
instance layer (Act~V) qualifies it: XGBoost and the foundation
models agree on 93.6\% to 95.0\% of instances (median across
datasets), the rank difference arises from a small fringe of
disagreements that TabFM wins on some datasets and loses on others,
and the three pre-registered explanations for the advantage were
not confirmed.

\textbf{In cost, the tie never existed.} Models practically
equivalent in accuracy (under the lenient criterion) differ by up to
about $300\times$ in training time, and the accuracy leader is the
grid's slowest at inference: 43{,}262~\us{} per row on
\texttt{adult}, against XGBoost's 0.33 --- inverting the cost axis
(seconds-long training and zero tuning; expensive serving).

These conclusions hold within four limits, declared where they bind:
few datasets per task (descriptive multiclass; p-value floor in
regression), a wide critical difference on the full grid, latency
measured in amortized batch with each model on its device, and TabFM
evaluated at a pinned version predating the peer review of its
technical report. Chapter~\ref{chap:framework} converts these
results into a constraint-based decision framework and evaluates it
--- out of sample for the learned component;
Chapter~\ref{chap:destilacao} investigates whether the foundation
model's latency can be reduced by distillation.
